title: Arthur Harari Explains Why The Unknown Used Deepfake Technology for a Léa Seydoux Scene
excerpt:
Arthur Harari confirms a controlled deepfake effect in The Unknown.
The filmmaker remains wary of AI taking over creative writing and decisions.
body_md:
Arthur Harari, director of The Unknown and an Oscar-winning co-writer of Anatomy of a Fall, has addressed the uneasy relationship between artificial intelligence and filmmaking. Speaking at the Marrakech Film Festival, he expressed strong reservations about AI in creative work while acknowledging that his latest film used a deepfake tool for a specific visual effect.

In conversation with film critic and historian Charles Tesson, Harari initially said he saw little place for AI in his own artistic practice. He described the technology as increasingly pervasive and tempting, warning that tools adopted for convenience can gradually influence the decisions artists make. His concern centers on creative dependence rather than the mere existence of new technology.

Harari then identified an exception in The Unknown. A scene depicts Léa Seydoux's character kissing another version of herself, requiring the production to employ deepfake technology. He emphasized that a human operator remained involved and in control. The distinction matters to his position: he does not reject every technical application, but questions when automation begins replacing artistic judgment.

He was more resistant to AI-generated writing. Basic research assistance, in his view, can be legitimate and useful, but allowing the technology to compose parts of a screenplay raises a different concern. Once a creative team becomes accustomed to delegating tasks, he suggested, resisting broader use can become progressively harder.

The Unknown stars Seydoux as a mysterious woman who spends a night with a photographer named David, played by Niels Schneider. The next morning, David discovers that he is trapped in her body. The psychological body-swap drama is based on a graphic novel co-written by Harari and screened in competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

Seydoux has previously described the part as among her most rewarding roles and voiced confidence that human creativity cannot simply be replaced by machines. The Marrakech Film Festival runs from November 20 through November 28, 2026. Harari's comments illustrate a distinction that is likely to remain central to filmmaking debates: the difference between carefully supervised visual tools and technology that begins to shape the substance of a creative work.
